Getting started with Programming using MOOCs.

I have been teaching myself to code and learning from MOOCs for the past year or so. The best way to learn programming is to dive in head first. Google is your best friend.

In my experience some of the hardest parts of programming are installing the various IDEs and SDKs needed for specific projects. I plan on posting a guide for some popular ones that tend to give beginners a hassle, like the Android SDK.

The beauty of starting on codecademy is that you don't have to worry about installing anything because the courses all have in browser coding environments. This is great for simple languages like Python, HTML, CSS, but can be a bit finicky for things like PHP. I consider codecademy more of a stepping stone for novice programmers. If you know absolutely nothing about progamming it is an amazing first step. For others, it should serve as a brief introduction to a language.

Choosing a starting point is intertwined with choosing the programming language you want to start with. I will eventually do some more detailed posts on each category I lay out here. When starting programming you'll want to identify your first goal as one of the following:

  1. Web Development
  2. Mobile Applications
  3. I just want to learn how to program

In this post I'll flesh out the tools for learning Web Development.

Web Development

HTML and CSS

When getting started on web development you'll always want to start with html. Web development consists of multiple interacting languages. After learning html, you can move onto CSS, or just start with the codecademy HTML & CSS course . It is usually a good idea to try and implement what you've learned on an actual website. Codecademy tends to give users a false sense of mastery that is crushed by the complex reality of most Web Development platforms. A good place to start is with a Wordpress Blog. Make One, pick a theme, download the custom CSS editor if your theme has no CSS field, and customize the shit out of that bad boy. Get acquainted with developer tools in Google Chrome, it will be your magic wand.

HTML Courses

  • w3Schools HTML Tutorial
  • HTML5 course on edX
  • codecademy HTML & CSS course
  • Code School HTML/CSS path

CSS Courses

  • w3Schools CSS Tutorial

Javascript

Alot of people may argue otherwise but I suggest you then move on to Javascript. This fuels clean website animations. One great way to start getting used to Javascript while also learning the woes of using an API, is to get Adobe Edge Animate (if you don't have the creative cloud you can always get EDGE from TPB.)

Javascript Courses

  • w3schools Javascript Course
  • codecademy Javavscript Course
  • Introduction to Bootstrap - edX
  • Code School Javascript path

jQuery, PHP, and SQL

Then move on to jQuery, PHP, and SQL. Honestly the best place to start is w3schools. You will want to essentially jump around as needed, you will understand why when you get to this point. And while you're on w3schools you can fill in gaps in your understanding of HTML and CSS. Once you know these six languages you're essentially in beast mode and can start learning cshtml, xml, and the other essentials for modern web design.

  • jQuery

PHP

  • w3Schools PHP Tutorial

Now hear me out, because it's easy to instantly poo-poo an idea like this.

We all like Voat because there's no restrictions on what people say here. But we also know the dark side of this kind of freedom; it will draw those with the time, passion and the inclination to use whatever tactics necessary to control the conversation and content. I'm talking about the kind of behaviour that most of us would consider odious: stalking users into unrelated comment threads to continue arguing; submitting large amounts of click-bait articles for the sole purpose of getting upvotes and/or stearing the content of a subverse closer to certain ideologies; going in to as many comment threads as possible, in whatever subverse, with the specific goal of talking endlessly about whatever their pet issue may be.

We're all aware that banning people or trying to enforce strict posting rules are not desirable solutions to these kind of problems. So what if there's a hard limit on comments and submissions? It doesn't have to be a very low limit; just enough to tone down the most egregious behavior. This would also need to be a limit that resets at a certain point each day, instead of being based on just the previous 24 hour window.

And on the plus side, it'll perhaps inspire some of the power users to get off the computer for a bit.

Anyway, food for thought. What do you all think?
Limiting upvotes/downvotes works. How about limiting comments/submissions?
